name: Gordon
history: A southern California apple from Whittier, in the Los Angeles basin, grown in home orchards for its low chill need and its long, drawn-out flowering and ripening. Its parentage and date are not well recorded.

look.description: Reported as green to yellow-green with red stripes and flush; fuller details not verified.

taste.summary: Described by Californian growers as crisp and juicy with a sweet-tart flavour, good both fresh and cooked; detailed tasting data are scarce.
taste.best_eaten: Through its long picking season (Aug-Oct in California)

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright tree with an unusually long bloom period, so it overlaps with many other varieties; fruit ripens over several weeks, which suits home growers.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded. Its long bloom makes it a useful partner for other low-chill apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild-winter, warm-summer regions such as coastal and inland southern California, where it ripens from August into October with about 400 chill hours.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter regions where early blossom is frosted, and cool short summers that cannot ripen its long-season crop.

grow_notes: A good backyard apple for mild-winter gardens, where its long bloom and staggered ripening spread the harvest. Give it room or prune hard, as it grows vigorously.

name: Lady Williams

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, probably of Granny Smith; the pollen parent is thought to be Jonathan or Rokewood.
origin.raised_by: Found on the orchard of Arthur and Maud Williams

history: Came up as a chance seedling around 1935 on the Williams family orchard at Donnybrook in Western Australia and was named after Maud Williams, who recognised its promise. Its fame rests on its offspring: crossed with Golden Delicious it gave Cripps Pink (Pink Lady) and Cripps Red.

look.description: Green apple turning yellowish-green, with a red to pinkish-red flush over part of the skin.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, dense flesh with a sharp, Granny Smith-like edge that rounds into a balanced sweet-sharp flavour after some months in store. A late, long-keeping apple rather than one to eat off the tree.

tree.notes: Needs a very long, warm growing season; in cool climates the fruit may not ripen before winter.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 2 (Orange Pippin); pair with another early-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm, sunny seasons with mild winters: south-west Western Australia, Mediterranean-type climates and the warmer apple districts of California and South Africa.
climate.poor_climates: Short or cool seasons: in places like the UK it ripens so late (November) that fruit is often under-ripe and exposed to frost.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented outside Australia.

grow_notes: Only worth planting where the season is long and warm enough to finish a very late apple. Pick as late as safely possible and store cold; flavour develops over the winter.

name: Democrat
history: A Tasmanian apple first recorded around 1900 and formerly grown in Australian orchards as a late-keeping dessert apple. Not to be confused with an older, unrelated American apple of the same name (also called Varick).

look.description: Dark red flushed apple; fuller details not verified.

taste.summary: Collection descriptions call the flesh crisp, sweet and juicy; detailed tasting notes are scarce.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not documented in sources available here.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; assume a compatible pollinator is needed.

climate.best_climates: Raised in Tasmania's cool-temperate maritime climate; likely to suit similar mild, moist apple regions. Chill figure is inferred from its origin.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; very hot or very cold climates are untested.

grow_notes: A heritage curiosity mainly found in Australian collections. Treat it as a typical late-season dessert apple and give it a long season to ripen.

name: Dunn's Favourite
history: No reliable record of an apple under this exact name was found. It may be a variant name for the Australian Dunn's Seedling, but that could not be confirmed, so this record is a placeholder.

taste.summary: No verified tasting notes are available for this name.

grow_notes: Identity unconfirmed; check the source of any tree sold under this name before planting.

name: Winter Banana
history: Found in 1876 on David Flory's farm in Cass County, Indiana, and introduced to the trade in 1890. Grown for its distinctive aroma and as a free-flowering pollinator, it is also unusually tolerant of mild winters for an old American apple.

look.description: Large, waxy pale-yellow apple with a soft pink to red blush on the sunny side; the skin marks and bruises easily.

taste.summary: Sweet, low-acid fruit with an unusual perfume; the banana note it is named for is subtle, obvious to some tasters and absent for others, and one grower found light pineapple tones. Texture reports differ: older descriptions call the flesh fairly tender and coarse, while growers describe it as dense and crisp, never mealy. The aroma builds as it mellows in store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb, after a few weeks in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, early-bearing spur type with tidy growth that needs little pruning. Its abundant blossom makes it a widely used pollinator.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4 (Orange Pippin). A generous pollen donor for other mid-to-late flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Unusually adaptable: grown in temperate regions down to about zone 5 and in mild-winter areas such as coastal California, where most older apples get too little chill (it needs about 300-400 hours).
climate.poor_climates: Humid regions with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure, since it is very susceptible; very cold zones below about zone 5.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; average resistance otherwise. The pale fruit bruises easily, so handle and store carefully.

grow_notes: A good pollinator and aromatic keeper for gardens from cool-temperate to mild-winter climates. Handle the fruit gently and keep it away from junipers where cedar-apple rust occurs.
